A1-A2.headline: The Mighty Battleships of the Sea

pages.text:
Big war ships with thick metal walls stood at the center of sea forces from the late 1880s.

Built to carry giant guns, these strong ships ruled the open seas for many years.
pages.caption: USS Iowa firing a large broadside.

evidence.fileTitle: File:BB61 USS Iowa BB61 broadside USN.jpg

pages.text:
The modern era of great war ships began in the late 1880s with Britain's Royal Sovereign ships. They had tall sides for rough ocean trips, thick metal skin, and a clear gun plan.

Other lands soon copied this strong style.
pages.caption: The German Brandenburg had six heavy guns.

evidence.articleCaption: The German Brandenburg, which carried six heavy guns, rather than the standard four

pages.text:
After the Russo-Japanese War, Britain built HMS Dreadnought and changed sea war forever. It carried ten giant guns of one size, leaving older ships out of date.

Soon, big nations raced to build even larger ships.
pages.caption: HMS Dreadnought was a new design.

pages.text:
After World War I, major nations signed agreements like the Washington Naval Treaty to limit how many giant war ships each side could build. Leaders hoped to stop expensive building races.

During World War II, fast war planes changed sea war once again. Planes could sink giant ships from far away, so big ships slowly lost their lead role.

Even as their sea power faded, these great war ships stayed proud symbols for their countries. Some experts had doubted their high price since the 1880s.

Today, several old ships remain open as floating museums.
pages.caption: USS Iowa sailing in the 1980s.

evidence.articleCaption: USN carrier group led by USS Iowa in 1987
evidence.articleSection: Cold War: end of the battleship era

B1-B2.headline: The Rise and Fall of the Great Battleships

pages.text:
Battleships were massive, heavily armored warships that formed the backbone of naval fleets from the late 1880s.

Armed with giant long-range guns, they were built to control the seas and win major ocean battles.
pages.caption: USS Iowa firing a full broadside.

evidence.fileTitle: File:BB61 USS Iowa BB61 broadside USN.jpg

pages.text:
The modern battleship era began in the late 1880s with Britain's Royal Sovereign class, known as pre-dreadnoughts.

Their high sides handled rough oceans well, pairing thick steel armor with a balanced set of guns.
pages.caption: The German Brandenburg carried six heavy guns.

evidence.articleCaption: The German Brandenburg, which carried six heavy guns, rather than the standard four

pages.text:
After the Russo-Japanese War, launching HMS Dreadnought transformed naval design. By using ten uniform heavy guns instead of mixed sizes, it made older fleets outdated.

The breakthrough soon sparked a costly global arms race.
pages.caption: HMS Dreadnought changed naval design forever.

pages.text:
After World War I, leading powers signed agreements such as the Washington Naval Treaty to cap battleship numbers and curb expensive naval rivalries.

During World War II, the rise of air power and aircraft carriers shifted naval warfare away from heavy gunships. Vulnerable to aerial attacks, battleships gradually lost their central role at sea.

Even as their fighting dominance declined, battleships remained dramatic symbols of national pride. Some naval experts had questioned their cost since the 1880s.

Today, surviving ships serve as historic museums around the world.
pages.caption: USS Iowa underway in 1987.

C1-C2.headline: The Evolution and Strategic Decline of the Capital Ship

pages.text:
Battleships were colossal, heavily armored capital warships constituting the backbone of major naval fleets from the late 1880s.

Engineered around large-caliber artillery, they embodied maritime supremacy across global oceans.
pages.caption: USS Iowa firing a full broadside.

evidence.fileTitle: File:BB61 USS Iowa BB61 broadside USN.jpg

pages.text:
The modern battleship lineage emerged in the late 1880s with Britain's Royal Sovereign pre-dreadnought class.

Combining high freeboard for oceanic endurance with heavy armor and standardized armament, they defined late-century naval design.
pages.caption: The German Brandenburg carried six heavy guns.

evidence.articleCaption: The German Brandenburg, which carried six heavy guns, rather than the standard four

pages.text:
Following the Russo-Japanese War, HMS Dreadnought revolutionized fleets with ten uniform heavy cannons.

Rendering older warships obsolete overnight, it ignited an intense international naval arms race.
pages.caption: HMS Dreadnought changed naval design forever.

pages.text:
After World War I, maritime powers negotiated accords such as the Washington Naval Treaty to restrict battleship tonnage and restrain ruinous naval expenditures.

During World War II, however, ascendant naval aviation and aircraft carriers eclipsed surface gunnery. Exposed to long-range aerial strikes, battleships relinquished their supremacy across modern fleets.

Even as tactical preeminence receded, battleships endured as potent emblems of national prestige despite skeptics advocating smaller vessels since the 1880s.

Today, preserved hulls operate as historic museum memorials worldwide.
